name: Drospirenone pill
lead: Drospirenone is a progestin with antiandrogen and antimineralocorticoid activity, related to the diuretic spironolactone. In pills combined with ethinylestradiol (Yasmin, Yaz and generics) it is prescribed for contraception and, in some jurisdictions, for moderate acne and premenstrual disorders.[1][8] For people interested in skin, the appeal is that blocking androgen receptors can reduce the oil production and breakouts that androgens drive, while its anti-fluid-retention action is described as counteracting the bloating associated with estrogen.[1]

Schering AG patented drospirenone in 1976 and it entered medical use in 2000 as a combined pill; later forms include a progestin-only pill (2019), an estetrol combination (2021) and an estradiol combination for menopause.[1] Wikipedia lists it among the most prescribed drugs in the United States, with more than 3 million prescriptions of the ethinylestradiol combination in 2023.[8]

Published research in the available literature centres on polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), where a systematic review compared drospirenone pills with other treatments,[2] and on contraception and cardiovascular questions. Documented risks include venous thromboembolism and raised potassium, and Bayer has faced thousands of lawsuits over clot risk.[1]

paras: The ethinylestradiol/drospirenone combination is indicated for moderate acne, premenstrual syndrome, premenstrual dysphoric disorder and painful periods, in addition to contraception.[1][8] The drospirenone component is the reason it is grouped among antiandrogenic pills, a class prescribed when acne or oily skin is considered hormone-related.[1]

The same combination is studied in PCOS, a condition with excess androgen features that include acne and excess hair growth.[2][3] Because drospirenone's mineralocorticoid-blocking action offsets estrogen-driven salt and water retention, Wikipedia says it helps maintain or slightly reduce body weight.[1]

Forms include a 4 mg progestin-only pill (Slynd), ethinylestradiol combinations (Yasmin, Yaz), an estetrol combination (Nextstellis) and an estradiol combination for menopausal symptoms and postmenopausal osteoporosis (Angeliq).[1] Versions with levomefolic acid (Beyaz, Safyral) add a folate component.[8] Drospirenone has also been used in hormone therapy for transgender women.[1]

A 2017 systematic review of 18 articles in women with PCOS reported that, compared with drospirenone alone, drospirenone plus metformin was better at reducing BMI, luteinizing hormone and LDL cholesterol; compared with metformin, drospirenone was better at modulating total testosterone, SHBG, FSH and the free androgen index, while metformin reduced BMI and lipids more.[2] In that review drospirenone was also reported to outperform cyproterone acetate for total cholesterol and insulin resistance.[2]

An uncontrolled study of 51 Indian women with PCOS taking ethinylestradiol with drospirenone followed them for six and twelve cycles and reported significant improvements in clinical and biochemical hyperandrogenic parameters, with no significant changes in BMI, abdominal circumference or metabolic measures.[3]

Drospirenone is a progesterone receptor agonist that suppresses ovulation, and an antagonist at the androgen and mineralocorticoid receptors.[1] In animals its antiandrogenic activity is about 30 percent that of cyproterone acetate, and 3 to 4 mg is described as roughly equivalent to 20 to 25 mg of spironolactone as an antimineralocorticoid.[1]

Wikipedia reports oral bioavailability of about 66 to 85 percent, peak levels 1 to 6 hours after dosing, 95 to 97 percent protein binding, metabolism largely independent of cytochrome P450, and an elimination half-life of 25 to 33 hours.[1]

Ethinylestradiol-containing pills raise venous thromboembolism risk, with absolute risk described as roughly 3 to 10 per 10,000 women per year, and some meta-analyses associating drospirenone pills with about 1.3 to 2.0 times the risk of levonorgestrel pills, though confounding may account for part of this.[1] Persistent hyperkalaemia requiring discontinuation occurred in about 0.2 percent of women taking 4 mg alone, and unscheduled bleeding was the most common effect of the progestin-only pill (40 to 64 percent), with acne in 3.8 percent and headache in 2.7 percent.[1]
Drospirenone products are contraindicated in renal or adrenal insufficiency, hepatic impairment and hyperkalaemia.[1] Data on breast cancer risk with newer progestins are limited.[1]

A 2017 systematic review of randomised trials in women with PCOS compared drospirenone pills with other standard treatments,[2] and an uncontrolled study of 51 women followed them for up to twelve cycles.[3] A completed phase 4 trial of 90 participants compared pills containing desogestrel and drospirenone for premenstrual symptoms,[11] and a trial of 32 participants examined an oral contraceptive for premenstrual worsening of depression.[12] Registered trials examine drospirenone-only pills for emergency contraception, after bariatric surgery, and in relation to blood pressure and vascular function.[4][5][6][7] None of these is an acne-specific trial.

Schering AG patented drospirenone in 1976 and received related patents in 1998 and 2000; it was introduced in 2000 in a pill with ethinylestradiol, approved with estradiol for menopause in 2005, as a progestin-only pill in 2019 and with estetrol in 2021.[1] Reported litigation: in July 2012 Bayer disclosed more than 12,000 suits over Yaz, Yasmin and related pills, with 1,977 cases settled for US$402.6 million at that point, and by 2015 about 10,000 claims had been settled without admission of liability.[1]

The pill is prescription-only in the United States, Canada and Australia.[1] Brand names include Yasmin and others for the 30 microgram version, Yaz, Yasminelle and Nikki for the 20 microgram version, and Beyaz and Safyral with levomefolic acid.[8]

On T Nation, members have discussed hormonal contraceptives' effect on appearance: one poster says Yasmin 'makes boobs huge' and that this was on the news, and another notes that Yasmin was supposed to cause less bloating than earlier pills.[9][10]

lore.intro: Community material on this pill is sparse and mostly concerns side effects people notice, such as bloating or breast size, in general-fitness forum discussion rather than looksmaxxing threads.[9][10]

claims.believers: A T Nation poster says she started Yasmin and within a week and a half her breasts had doubled, adding that it had been on the news.[9]
claims.experts: No published trial of drospirenone pills for breast size exists, and Wikipedia notes data on breast outcomes with newer progestins are limited.[1]

claims.claim: Yasmin causes less bloating than other pills.
claims.believers: A T Nation member writes that hormonal contraceptives cause bloating and that Yasmin is supposed to be better in this regard.[10]
claims.experts: Drospirenone blocks the mineralocorticoid receptor, which counters estrogen-driven fluid retention, and Wikipedia says it helps maintain or slightly reduce body weight.[1]

card.summary: An antiandrogenic birth-control progestin that is indicated for moderate acne in some regions, with most published research focused on PCOS.
card.note: Raises potassium and carries a venous clot risk; prescription only.

quick.overview:
Drospirenone is a progestin in contraceptive pills such as Yasmin and Yaz. Because it also blocks androgen receptors, the ethinylestradiol combination is indicated for moderate acne in some jurisdictions.
The studies are mostly in PCOS and contraception rather than acne itself.
quick.mechanism: It suppresses ovulation as a progestin, blocks androgen receptors, and blocks the mineralocorticoid receptor like spironolactone.
quick.risks: Combined pills raise clot risk; some studies suggest higher risk than levonorgestrel pills. Drospirenone can raise potassium. Prescription only.

chain: Clearer skin in people prescribed the pill for acne
angle.text: A low-dose ethinylestradiol/drospirenone pill is indicated for moderate acne in some jurisdictions. People use it, under prescription, for the antiandrogen effect on oily, breakout-prone skin, often alongside its contraceptive and premenstrual uses.
